games.explanation: Bailey Ober has spent the year giving right-handed hitters a soft place to land, and the White Sox happen to trot out a lineup full of them at a plus price nobody wants to touch. Vargas and Benintendi have both been sharper against righties than their overall lines suggest, and Ober's barrel rate against righty bats is the kind of number that turns quiet nights into three-run innings. Fedde is no one's idea of an ace, but Minnesota's middle order is more churn than thunder, and the park is playing generous enough to reward the team swinging with the platoon edge. At +108 on the better side of an Elo gap this wide, the market is basically shrugging. Take the shrug.

The market is pricing this like Chicago is a tier above Cincinnati, when the actual gap is a coin flip with a slightly better logo. Abbott has quietly been the sharper arm of the two starters this year, and a park that suppresses runs and a wind blowing straight in is not the environment where the Cubs bury anyone. Elly gets a righty he can do damage against, and the sim spits out a one-run game that ends 4-3 either way. Getting a run and a half at -125 in a projected 4.4 to 4.3 grinder is how you print tickets without needing to be right about the winner.

Baltimore is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but a run and a half is a lot of insurance against a Shane Baz who has spent the year handing right-handed hitters a batting practice fastball. His splits versus righties are ugly in the exact ways that matter, a barrel rate north of 13% and hard contact on nearly half the balls in play, and the Athletics happen to run a righty-heavy top of the order into that buzzsaw. Jack Perkins isn't going to out-duel anyone, but he misses enough bats to keep this from turning into the laugher the market is pricing. Our sim lands on a one-run game, and getting a run and a half at a shade above even money is the whole point.
